import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjectures associated with A109909

$a(n)$ = number of primes of the form $k(n-k)-1$.

*References:*
- [A109909](https://oeis.org/A109909)
-/

namespace OeisA109909

/--
$a(n)$ is the number of primes of the form $k(n-k)-1$.
This counts the number of distinct prime values in the set $\{k(n-k)-1 | 1 \le k < n\}$.
-/
def a (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.Ico 1 n).image (fun k => k * (n - k) - 1)
  |>.filter Nat.Prime
  |>.card

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_1 : a 1 = 0 := by decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_2 : a 2 = 0 := by decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_3 : a 3 = 0 := by decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_4 : a 4 = 2 := by decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_5 : a 5 = 2 := by decide

/--
Conjecture: $a(n) > 0$ for $n > 3$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem conjecture : ∀ n > 3, a n > 0 := by
  sorry

end OeisA109909

reformulations.difference: The definition uses every k with 1 ≤ k < n and counts distinct prime values using Finset.image. The related OEIS algorithms use the half-range 1 ≤ k ≤ floor(n/2).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The substitution k ↦ n−k preserves k(n−k)−1 and takes every upper-half index to the half-range. Thus both ranges have exactly the same image. On the half-range the polynomial is injective: for k < l ≤ n/2 its increase is (l−k)(n−k−l) > 0. Consequently the Lean cardinality also equals the number of prime-producing half-range indices. I proved this equality for every natural n and the resulting conjecture biconditional in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean, without sorry or reliance on the conjecture.

sources_consulted: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A109/A109909.seq — OEIS A109909, including its terms, conjecture, verification comment, and references.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A026/A026728.seq — related prime-counting sequence, examples, and half-range algorithms.

review.notes: Checked all seven declarations. All 93 published sequence terms match Lean evaluation, including the five test theorems. Checked a(0)=0 and found no zero values for 4 ≤ n ≤ 1000. Proved that natural-number subtraction agrees with the integer polynomial whenever 1 ≤ k < n. The main theorem exactly matches OEIS's 'Conjecture: a(n) > 0 for n > 3.' The entry still calls it a conjecture and reports verification through 10^9, so no status discrepancy was identified. OEIS content was read through its data mirror because its HTML endpoints returned Cloudflare challenges. The linked Niu–Zhang paper was access-restricted; only its DOI metadata was available, and its contents were not reviewed. Experiments are in /workspace/review/; the target file was not changed.
